utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, once again I remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you took, you made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: As always, please tell me if you're unable to understand me or if you don't understand one of my questions.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yesterday when we finished --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm just noticing that we are not getting the transcript on the e-court which will cause a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right, on our monitors. We are not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On our monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- we are not getting the transcript and that will eventually cause a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It will catch up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The report we get is that somebody is coming to try and fix this problem, a technician, but it doesn't -- we don't know how long it will take. Mr. Whiting, you say there will be problems if we continue without the LiveNote?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I think I can do it. It's just I keep track of the transcript on this monitor and the exhibits on this monitor but I'll manage. It's fine. We can -- it's being transcribed, it's being recorded. We have a record. It will just be a minor inconvenience for me but that's fine. I can manage. We can proceed. I don't want to delay the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But if you then should have video showing here or video recording what are you going to do? Then you won't be having any transcript on the monitor, if you want to show something on the other screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's all right. That's fine. That will be fine. I'll manage, Your Honour. I'll just be able to switch back and forth and it will be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Very well then. We may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Should I proceed, your honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, when we finished yesterday, we had listened to two intercepts. I'd like to listen to one more at the moment. And if we could look at number 93, which I believe is the third one in the packet, do you see that one, Mr. Babic, 93?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On the declaration that you signed, you identified the voices in this intercept as being Radovan Karadzic and Slobodan Milosevic. You've told us already about your interactions with Radovan Karadzic, and to a large extent also with Slobodan Milosevic, but could you just remind us again approximately how many times did you meet with Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than 20 times, about 20 times, until the end of 1991, and then a couple of other times afterwards, about five to six meetings and contacts up until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to speak with him on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to hear his voice also in the media?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, could you take a moment to look at this conversation and are you able to tell us generally what this conversation is about, to your understanding?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about the events which took place after the Croatian parliament as well as the Republic of Slovenia declared the independence of those two states after the referenda, and after the point in time when the European Union got involved in the conflict solving. As of then, the EU took on an active role in the search for solutions and tried to solve the problems arising from the former Yugoslavia, and the rest of the conversation refers to a meeting between Milosevic and Mikelis [phoen]. It was on that occasion that this conversation took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to try to play a clip and hopefully it will work. We tested it again last night and it worked when we tested it but we will see if it will work here in the courtroom. And the clip that I want to play, it starts on -- on the English it starts on the bottom of page 1 where Radovan Karadzic says, "Yes, yes." And on the B/C/S, Mr. Babic, it's on page 2. You'll see about a third of the way down, Mr. Radovan Karadzic says, "Yes, yes, what can make additional problems?" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I wonder if the AV booth needs to switch us over to Sanction so that we can hear the sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, in that clip, Slobodan Milosevic says, "That's clear and they should be allowed to separate." And then he says, "now there is only one question left, to have disintegration in the line with our inclinations." What do you understand him to be talking about in that section?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already mentioned that Croatia and Slovenia arrived at the decision to secede. In this particular case, the discussion is about Croatia. The European Union suggested for that secession or rather the decision on that secession to be postponed by three months and that was agreed. And the conversation is about this three-month period which is supposed to run. At that point in time, Mr. Izetbegovic and Gligorov were putting forward solutions referring to federations -- confederations, an asymmetrical confederation -- compromise solutions for this crisis. And as to this attitude on the part of Milosevic, that they should be allowed to secede, in other words it was that Croatia should be allowed to go independent, to secede, and then he goes on to say that this secession line, line of secession, needs to be the one that suits us. What he means to say is that they can go but are not allowed to take those territories that he himself and Serbs in general considered should remain within this new state in which Serbs would live. So basically, it meant that they would not have been allowed to take Krajina, that SAO Krajina and other parts of Croatian territory would be kept and would be kept separate from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Gligorov. Could you tell us who those two people were at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Izetbegovic was the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Kiro Gligorov was the president of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is having read through this transcript and listened to it, Mr. Babic, is it consistent with the views that you, as you knew them, of Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Milosevic at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And based on your knowledge and understanding of the time, is there anything that causes you in looking at this transcript and intercept to question its authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this exhibit, which is 93, be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By the way, that's a 65 ter 93?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Exhibit 65 ter 93 is admitted into evidence, may it please be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be marked for identification, 202, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And we can put the bundle, the intercept bundle away for now. I won't be using it until later. I'm also happy to report that the transcript is now working.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I'd like to talk to you about a different subject now. I'd like to talk to you about the JNA and the control over the JNA. During 1991, who commanded the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A civilian command was in the hands of the Presidency of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and when there was imminent danger of war or a state of war, the command would come from the Supreme Command Staff, the General Staff of the armed forces of Yugoslavia and the federal Secretary for Defence. And the actual control as far as I know over the JNA I mean, since July, was in the hands of Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: July of what year -- of which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how did he do that? How did Slobodan Milosevic control the JNA after July of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, in two ways. First of all he had a part of the presidency under his control, the so-called rump Presidency of the SFRJ which formally represented the Supreme Command and he had direct influence over the General Command Staff, that is to say the generals and the federal secretary, Veljko Kadijevic and Blagoje Adzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take those two one at a time and I'm going to take it step by step. And some of these questions may seem a bit basic to you but they will be of assistance to us. The Presidency of the SFRY, how was that composed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each republic and Autonomous Region of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia had a member, had a seat on the Presidency. One of the members of the Presidency would be president for a year, according to a preordained order. So there was a rotation every year and there was a new president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia every year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And am I correct that there were six republics and two autonomous regions and therefore eight positions on the Presidency? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And during 1990 and 1991, who was the president of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since May 1990, until December -- or rather the 12th of May 1991, it was Borisav Jovic, who was a member of the Presidency representing Serbia. And between May 1991 until October, the 3rd of October, 1991, formally speaking it was Stipe Mesic or rather for a while he did not carry out those duties. For a while he did. It was a Presidency crisis, in fact. As of October 1991, up until the setting up of the federal Republic of Serbia in April 1992, the so-called rump Presidency was in operation. It had four members, and it was presided by the deputy president, Branko Kostic who represented Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And earlier in response to one of my questions, you said that Slobodan Milosevic had a part of the Presidency under his control. Which part of the Presidency specifically?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Jovic, who was the representative of Serbia, Branko Kostic from Montenegro, and the representatives of the autonomous regions, Mr. Bajramovic from Kosovo and the Vojvodina representative I can't recall his name right now. I'll try and remember it. So it was since spring basically that those changes started being made. So I think that this reflected the situation as of May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the rump Presidency that you referred to, was that comprised of those four members that you've just identified?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Jugoslav Kostic from Vojvodina, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what happened to the other four members of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since October, they no longer participated in the work of the Presidency. Stipe Mesic declared that Yugoslavia no longer existed and that there was no place for him there, and I think that the representative of Macedonia attended one meeting in the beginning of October and none later, and as of October no other representatives participated, no other representatives of any other republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you also said when you were explaining how Milosevic had control over the JNA, that he had control over the generals or influence over the generals. Can you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he boasted himself in the beginning of July that he had control over the JNA, and also in the beginning of July, I met two generals at his cabinet, Kadijevic and Adzic, in particular, who came to talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is July of what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Tell us please about how he boasted in the beginning of July that he had control over the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was invited to his cabinet for an interview, for a talk, and Radovan Karadzic was there, and we were supposed to work on the solution of the problem created by the declaration which referred to the unification of SAO Krajina and Bosanska Krajina, and at the end of that conversation, as we were leaving, Milosevic said wait a second and he went to an adjoining room and he came back and he was carrying a piece of paper, he didn't tell us what it was but standing at the door, he looked at us in a very self-assured way, and he said, "Where should I deploy the armed forces?" And he looked at me and I said, "along the Krajina borders." And then he looked at Karadzic and he said, "Along the borders to Croatia and then we'll sort things out with them afterwards." And that was the end of the conversation. And then he nodded. He didn't actually say anything. He just nodded. That was his farewell. I think he wanted to make us aware of the fact that he had control over the armed forces rather than ask us where to deploy them because he must have had his own plans by then. Immediately after that, or at the next meeting, we found the generals there at his cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Tell us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Milosevic invited me to Belgrade, to his cabinet, and I did, and his secretary said, "The Presidency -- the president is in a meeting with the generals. He won't be able to see you. Just wait here." And it was the adjoining room, next to his office, and she opened the door and President Milosevic came out and he said to me, well, there were two generals sitting there and I knew their faces from the media and he said to me that he was in a meeting with them and that he wasn't able to see me. And so I went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Which generals were there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kadijevic and Adzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And tell us again what their positions were at the time.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kadijevic was the federal Secretary for People's Defence, and General Blagoje Adzic was the chief of the General Staff of the armed forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. Or rather, if there was imminent danger of war or a state of war it was the staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the SFRJ. They were the top guys.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us earlier in your testimony that frequently when you visited Mr. Milosevic, he would talk to you about what the army would do for the Serbs in Krajina. Could you remind us again what it is he said on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said, "Don't worry, the JNA will protect you." That was his slogan, that he kept repeating almost every time, except for a period of time in March and April 1991. That was when there was a different turn of events. But throughout the rest of the time, ever since I first met him, up until July and even later, he kept convincing us that we, the Serbs in Croatia, and since I was from the SAO Krajina, so that included us as well, that we would be protected by the JNA, from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to talk now about some events during the spring and summer of 1991. Were there armed clashes between the police of the SAO Krajina and Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflicts started on the 31st of March 1991, at Plitvice. That was a big conflict. And it continued up until open war in August or rather war actually started in June, by the end of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did the JNA respond to these clashes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA according to plan was deployed between the warring factions. They were holding the so-called buffer zone between the warring parties of Krajina and Croatia, in the periods of time between April or perhaps as early as March and that's the bit I'm not all that familiar with but at any rate between April 1991 and August 1991. In that period of time, the JNA was in charge of the so-called buffer zone between the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that this was done according to plan. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to plan, in the same way. Simply according to plan. I'm not saying that I saw a layout or an actual plan of deployment, but the JNA always deployed itself in the same way after incidents and provocations. Staged by the police of Krajina, the JNA would always come out or rather first the Croatian police would respond and then the JNA would deploy itself in a buffer zone. That was the pattern from Plitvice on to Zadar all the way up to Vukovar, as far as I heard, in the entire territory of Croatia, wherever conflicts happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, let me just get clear on the pattern that you've described. Provocations would be staged by the police of Krajina, the Croatian police would respond, and then the JNA would deploy as a buffer. Is that the pattern?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's the pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you referred to -- you've already referred to something that happened at Plitvice on the 31st of March 1991, and for the benefit of the Chamber, Plitvice appears on page 19 of the atlas, on the right side, about two-thirds of the way down. Before we talk about that event I want to show you a document, and if we could look at 65 ter Exhibit 244, and specifically 02170646, because there are several documents that are contained within 244. That's 0644. Could we have 0646?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are still trying to find Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's at approximately E3 on the map, just above E3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it the same thing as Plitvice? Okay. Plitvice above that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you. Apparently there is some difficulty pulling up the B/C/S version so I have a -- always prepared, I have a hard copy of it. Is the English version up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Forget about the English version. We just can't get anything on the main monitor. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you see that document? Are you able -- it's a little small. Are you able to read it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you raise it a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could it be made a little larger for the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. What's the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 15th February 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who is it from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's from the Secretariat of the Interior of Knin, the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina. It is addressed to the Presidency of the SFRY in Belgrade, federal Secretariat for the Interior in Belgrade, federal Secretariat of Defence in Belgrade, the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia in Zagreb and the republic Secretariat of the Interior of the socialist Republic of Serbia in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It looks like we are looking at something completely different the we are looking at a document dated the 3rd of March 1991 and it is not addressed to all of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, on the B/C/S, that is the document. But they have put the wrong translation up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Because as he speaks we try -- we can't read B/C/S so we try to check what he says by looking at the English version so if we are getting a wrong document on the English version, we are not able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we put -- is possible to put the correct translation, 0646, on the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay, that's it now. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's better. Now we are with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Babic, you said the Secretariat -- it was from the Secretariat of the Interior of Knin. Just to be clear, who was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an organ of the Serb Autonomous District of Krajina, the police led by Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. I was looking for who led it. That's all. And do you know -- are you familiar with what this document is about, what it's talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that incident and it's described here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you explain it to us, what this is about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have a precise description here. In the area of Plitvice lakes, Titova Korenica, there was a special unit of the MUP of Croatia of about 150 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to that special unit? Did it stay there in Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They withdrew after a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've already referred to an event that occurred on the 31st of March 1991. Did they withdraw before the 31st of March 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour? I'm sorry, I've just been signalled it's already in, as Exhibit 105.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us what happened on the 31st of March in Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the first major armed conflict between the police of Krajina and the police of Croatia, with casualties. Men were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how did it come about? Do you remember what happened, that brought it about? Step by step?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to that, the government of Croatia had announced that in the area of Plitvice lakes, a special separate municipality would be organised. They would excise the Plitvice lakes from the Titova Korenica municipality, which was in SAO Krajina. We in SAO Krajina thought about that and we agreed that the best thing to do would be to show the formal presence of SAO Krajina in Plitvice lakes to demonstrate that Plitvice lakes were part of SAO Krajina, by opening a regular police station at Plitvice lakes to maintain public law and order. I discussed the matter with Mr. Martic, with Dusan Orlovic who was assistant for state security, and I informed them of that position of the political leadership of Krajina and they did promise that they would open a regular police station there. However, that did not happen. Instead, the police of Krajina were sent there and they were deployed in a combat disposition, facing Croat territory along the bridge and facing the woods near Slunj. The Croatian government responded by sending in special police units whose task was to occupy the area of Plitvice by force, and that's what happened. A skirmish occurred between the police of Krajina and the Croat special police. There was a great upheaval, rallying of volunteers, panic, and distress among the Serbs because it looked like Croatia was launching a major offensive to take over the territory of Krajina. Five hours from the start of this skirmish, around 5 p.m., it was actually more than five hours later, in the areas of Jezera village and Plitvice lakes, an armoured mechanised unit of the JNA appeared. I think they came from the drill grounds of Slunj. They belonged originally to the Zagreb army district, and they deployed themselves there. In the days that followed, the political leadership of Krajina responded with a political provocation aimed at Serbia and Milosevic, demanding that he protect the Krajina population. This provocation took the shape of a decision by the political leadership of Krajina to officially join Serbia and to demand assistance from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I'm going to ask you about that last part of your answer in a moment but first I want to ask you about something you said earlier which is that men were killed. Do you know how many men were killed in this event?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two dead. One Croat policeman and one Serb policeman. In fact, what was being said was that the Serb person was a civilian. I'm not sure. I know that there was one dead on each side. However, the reports from Korenica spoke about a large number of dead, captured, wounded, and that caused a lot of panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So these reports from Korenica that spoke about a large number of dead and captured and wounded, were they inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that the JNA intervened. Did the JNA act as a buffer afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the 31st of March until end August or maybe early September. I'm not quite sure. It acted as a separation force, as a buffer zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what happened at the end of August or early September? Did something change?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The JNA moved into an offensive against the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the result of that offensive, if you know, at Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they put under the control -- under control the area of Plitvice lakes, resulting in the flight or expulsion of Croat population. It was a military takeover of that area, and its annexation to Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, was there also an event that occurred at Pakrac around this time, that is in the spring of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The events in Pakrac took place around the 31st of March 1991. At the time I was in Belgrade, I had just come back from an international conference in Geneva. I was holding a press conference, and I had to stay in Belgrade for a while. So I heard about this incident from reports, from the press, and a bit from Slobodan Milosevic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the date again that it took place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around the 1st of March 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So approximately a month before Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what happened, to your knowledge, at Pakrac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, Serb armed units took over the municipal assembly by force, and they took over the entire town of Pakrac and its environs. I don't know what the scale of this was. There was a response from the Croatian police and authorities. The press reported a large number of dead and wounded. The reports in the Belgrade press, TV, and other media were very dramatic. The Yugoslav People's Army got involved in these events. They deployed themselves in the area of Pakrac. I don't know exactly in which positions. Hearing about this, I called up Mr. Milosevic on the phone asking him what was going on, and telling him I was upset. He said, "Don't worry, everything is fine. You can go to Knin." Later, I heard that the press had exaggerated. I heard that the press -- I remember the press wrote about Savo Bosanac being there as one of the major figures and I later heard that it was untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you later learn if anybody had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, you didn't learn, or, no, nobody was killed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose nobody was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why do you suppose that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't get any verified information about anybody getting killed. In fact, I'm not familiar with the precise details.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you made reference going back to the events that occurred at the end of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I ask something? You were speaking of the press. What newspapers or what kind of media was that? The press in Krajina or in Serbia? What are you referring to? If you could give a little detailed information, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Belgrade newspapers and television. Krajina did not have its own press. At that time I was in Belgrade myself and I was reading Belgrade newspapers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I want to go back to the events in Plitvice on the 31st of March. You said when you were describing them that you afterwards caused a political provocation with Serbia and you described the decision to annex to Serbia -- I think we have evidence about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd like, if we could, to look at 65 ter Exhibit 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a document we sent to the addresses indicated above. The Presidency of the SFRY, the staff of the JNA command, the federal Secretariat of the Interior and other federal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And why did you send this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, concerning the events in Plitvice and based on the information I had about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In point 1, it says that you urge the addressees to urgently and entirely implement the decision of the Presidency of Yugoslavia on complete withdrawal of aggressor and terrorist forces of MUP, of so-called Republic of Croatia, from the territory of SAO Krajina. What decision are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a prior decision of the Presidency, I'm not sure if it was a decision of the Presidency or the president of the Presidency for the warring parties to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At the time you sent this, had the JNA already deployed in Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 203, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, after the events in Plitvice, during April, May and June, and even into July of 1991, were there continued clashes between the police of the SAO Krajina and the police of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were constant skirmishes on the contact lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did these skirmishes follow the pattern that you described earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from what I know, yes. The police and the armed units from Krajina staged provocations against police stations of Croatia and populated areas with Croat population. There were skirmishes. Policemen were arrested. The conflicts intensified and then the JNA intervened to separate the parties. That occurred in the area of Krajina and on the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, yesterday you said that in the spring of 1991, Mr. Martic made a number of statements in the media about the security situation in the SAO Krajina and about arrests. And I'd like to show you a few articles and see if you could comment on them. For this I'm going to need the assistance of the usher and we'll do it on the ELMO. They are not in e-court; I have them in hard copy and I also have them only in English but I'll read portions for the witness. The first article is from the BBC summary and it's dated April 4th of 1991. And I'll just read you two portions of it, Mr. Babic. In the second line it says, "According to him," Milan Martic, "the Krajina Police have arrested six Croatian constables. Four were arrested on 31 March near Plaski, municipality of Otocac and two on the 1st, 2nd April near Civljane." Then at the end of the article it says, "Martic also said that citizens are already bringing into the police station in Knin lists of those capable of bearing arms, that about 10.000 people from Krajina are on these lists, so far, and that further lists are still arriving. At the protest meeting in Knin late on 1st April, Martic said that the president of Serbia has promised that he would send arms to Krajina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Whiting, what are you reading? We have -- what we have on our screen here is this thing titled, copyright 1991, the British Broadcasting Corporation, BBC summary of world broadcasts for April 14, 1991, Thursday. From then on whatever you have read we don't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I read the second line of the text and then the last line of the text. The last two lines of the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The second line of the text would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Starting as "according to him the Krajina Police" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then the last two lines at the bottom. I'm sorry I wasn't clear about that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The last two lines at the bottom, if you can go up so that we can see the last two lines at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could the usher just push the document a little bit up on the ELMO? It's the last two lines of that second paragraph, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, did you hear what I read out from this article?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you -- it refers to constables who were arrested near Plaski and two near Civljane. Can you tell us where those places are?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Plaski is in Lika, between Lika and Kordun. Whereas Civljane is a place in the area of the municipality of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is this article consistent with the reporting, the reporting in the media and statements of Mr. Martic, that you heard at the time, that you described earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the news and the communiques issued at Mr. Martic's press conferences.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 204, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have a second article to show, with the assistance of the usher. The ERN of this article is R 0297428 to 7429. This is an article from Belgrade Tanjug dated the 26th of July 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell us, Mr. Babic, what is Tanjug?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the state news agency of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In the third paragraph of the text, and I'll just read it, it says, "Police chief in the Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina, Milan Martic, said today in Knin that his militia would not withdraw from the Sibenik area." And then the skipping one paragraph, it says, "Martic said that 'fierce conflicts were expected over the next few days.' And that in battles near Glina, three Krajina Militiamen were slightly wounded and'another 20 Croatian policemen had been arrested in the Banija and Kordun area.'" Mr. Babic, first of all, where is the -- can you describe for us where the Sibenik area is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sibenik is the adjacent municipality of the municipality of Knin and it lies along the coast.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is this article consistent with the reporting and statements of Mr. Martic that you described in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with his statements and with the events that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this article be given a number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: A number?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could it be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 205, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at 65 ter Exhibit 109? Which is Exhibit 31 in evidence. Sorry, yes, it's Exhibit 38. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, is there a document on the screen in front of you? Because our screen is -- there is nothing on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the letterhead, the upper part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we scroll down on this document so that we can see the top of it, please, I'm sorry, see the top of the document? There.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document or do you need to see more of it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is a report sent by the TO staff, addressed to the Supreme Commander SAO Krajina TO, Secretary SAO Krajina SUP, state security department, TO Commander, and Frenki, dated the 5th and the 6th of August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you receive this report at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In the -- if we could scroll down, in the second paragraph, it says, "There was an armed clash between our forces and the Ustashas in the village of Lovinac in Gracac. Some tanks left Gospic for Gracac to create a buffer zone. During the morning, our forces opened fire on the Ustasha positions at Otocac, Saborsko, and Sinac and according to our information heavy casualties were inflicted on the enemy." Then down a little further, it says, "According to information from the DB, 11 people were killed and 25 wounded during fighting in the Velika Glava and Bratiskovci area and several buildings were destroyed." Do you remember hearing about those events?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The reference to the DB is to which DB, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is state security, a part of the Ministry of the Interior of the SAO Krajina. That is the unified DB, including the Serb one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to the top of the document, there, that first paragraph, it says underneath the date which is 5th, 6th August 1991, "Due to the visit of the SFRY vice-president, Branko Kostic, and the peace delegation, Milan Martic has issued an order for a cease-fire except in the event of a direct attack." Why is Milan Martic issuing an order for a cease-fire at this time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, he commanded the armed forces or as it was referred to among the Serb public, the armed resistance of the Serb people against the newly appointed Croatian fascist authorities. And the delegation of the federal authorities was supposed to come in, in order to establish some sort of truce. The delegation was headed by a member of the Presidency, Mr. Branko Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is already in evidence so I won't move it in, and I'm done with this document so it can be taken off the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By the way, the document, one of the addressees of the document was Frenki, and who did you understand that to be, Frenki?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Franko Simatovic, aka, Frenki, an employee with the DB of Serbia. I spoke about him yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You did. What was the result of that delegation coming to the SAO Krajina? Was there a truce?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for a brief period, I believe so, perhaps up until the 18th -- excuse me, for two or three weeks in August, until the 25th or the 26th of August. I'm certain about the area of Knin, not equally certain about some other parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. You testified yesterday about -- and the day before, about the parallel structure and about the relationship between Milan Martic and the Ministry of the Interior in the SAO Krajina and the Ministry of the Interior in Serbia and you've also referred to Jovica Stanisic and you told us what positions he held. Did you see Jovica Stanisic in the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On what occasions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time was in August 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a restaurant called Vrelo as one enters the village of Golubic. He was there with Mr. Martic or to be more precise, Mr. Martic invited me to come and meet someone from the SUP of Serbia. It was still the time when the barricade staff at Golubic was functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did he tell you why he wanted you to meet someone from the SUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said something to the effect that it was a friend, someone who could help. At first I was a bit taken aback. I didn't trust him completely and I remained rather cool, and soon I forgot all about that event until January 1991, when Stanisic actually reminded me in Belgrade that he was the person I met in August, and who was with Martic at Vrelo restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did you meet Mr. Stanisic in Belgrade in January of 1991? How did that come about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information prior to that that a military coup was to be staged in Croatia and that the political leadership of Croatia was to be removed and a military regime established. After that, I was invited by Milosevic, who told me that he will arrest Martin Spegelj and some Croatian ministers in Zagreb and that I was under threat in Knin and that I should stay in Belgrade under their protection and control. He told me to go and see the minister or rather the Secretariat of the Interior, Mr. Radmilo Bogdanovic and that I should seek protection with him and that I should remain in Belgrade. After that I went to see Mr. Radmilo Bogdanovic to the Ministry of the Interior in Serbia and he asked me where I lived, where I was it stay, and I cited my cousin's address. He told me to go and see Jovica Stanisic, who was an employee with the state security in the old building that was just adjacent to the ministry building. They took me through some corridors between the two buildings and I finally met Jovica Stanisic who then said that he would provide me with an escort from the state security. And I remained a fortnight in Belgrade protected by the state security of Serbia. At a certain point I decided to leave because there were rumours in Knin that I had fled. Spegelj in the end was not arrested. Nothing was done, and Radmilo Bogdanovic told me "It is best if you return to your own people." And that's how my stay in Belgrade concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, after the break I'm going to ask you about other meetings that you had with Jovica Stanisic, both in -- at the SAO Krajina and in Belgrade but we have reached the time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break and come back at quarter to 11. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, before the break, we were talking about occasions when you saw Jovica Stanisic. And I'd like to focus first on occasions when you saw him in the SAO Krajina. You told us about the first time in August of 1990. When is the next time you saw him in the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my apartment in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened? Can you describe the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He arrived with another person. He introduced him as Frenki. He said that Frenki was an electronics expert, something of such nature, and he said that they were there to check my apartment to see whether it was being tapped by the army. That was the event. After that, Frenki arrived with a group of people and they searched the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that Frenki Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And why would your apartment have been tapped by the army, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume that that was one of their routine tasks. The KOS, the counterintelligence department was in charge of that and I could have been of some interest to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you see Jovica Stanisic in the SAO Krajina on any other occasions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the SAO Krajina, I saw him two more times, in early August 1991, at least that was the second time I saw him, as far as I can remember, in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what was the occasion of that meeting or seeing him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time we met was by chance, on the 1st or the 2nd of August. That is immediately after my proposal and after the government of the SAO Krajina disbanded the state security service. The next time was after Captain Dragan left, so it may have been a couple of days after that. In any case, both events took place in a relatively short time. It was the meeting held at the same cafe, at the Vrelo cafe at Golubic where we met the first time and, apart from himself, Mr. Dusan Orlovic was present as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You described earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: And Mr. Martic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, who was present there? Was it Mr. Orlovic or Mr. Martic or both?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And were they present for the second meeting in August?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the second and only meeting in August. The first one was by chance when I met Stanisic in the street and he was by himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You described earlier in your testimony a conversation that you had with Jovica Stanisic about your decision of August 1st 1991 to disband the DB in the SAO Krajina. Did that occur when you met him by chance in the street or did that conversation occur at the cafe?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met by chance in the street, or at least it seemed so. He may have been there waiting for me to see me, but we didn't discuss that at the cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you described -- well, let me ask you this first. Do you know what the relationship was between Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Martic? What kind of relationship did they have?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite friendly, they cooperated closely, and Martic listened carefully to what Stanisic had to say. It wasn't any sort of formal subordination but rather taking advice from a senior colleague. It didn't involve any sort of obedience.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what relationship did Mr. Stanisic have with Mr. Milosevic, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was his subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you described a meeting that occurred with Mr. Stanisic in January of 1991. Did you see -- did you have occasion to see Mr. Stanisic again in Belgrade, later that year?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him in March 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you describe the circumstances of that meeting? What happened then? Why were you in Belgrade? What was happening?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was end March 1991. Before that, there was the crisis with the Yugoslav Presidency and they didn't pass the decision on the introduction of state of emergency and the deployment of the JNA, and Borisav Jovic resigned temporarily with the Presidency and then he was returned and re-established, when it became clear that there was a serious crisis in the functioning of the state leadership and the JNA, Mr. David Rastovic came to see me. He was the president of the Donji Lapac municipality. He said that we were urgently to go and see Mr. Milosevic, to ask him what his ideas were as concerns our protection under such circumstances and that was the reason for the meeting, and we asked to see Milosevic. He received us in Belgrade in his cabinet office, and we asked him what we should do, and that we felt unsafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said it was the first time he mentioned any sort of JNA protection, and he also said, "I purchased 20.000 pieces of weapons in Hungary for you". And we just looked at each other, and we said "We have no idea what you're talking about." And then David Rastovic left the room to look for someone else. I forgot this person's name. He was a retiree who lived in Belgrade but originated from Krajina. He was a civilian with some function, I can't actually recall, and he wanted to ask him whether he knew anything of what Milosevic was saying because I presumed he had a role to play in the purchase of weapons. He also came to Milosevic's office and he said that nothing was done. Then Milosevic uttered some rather strong words and he said they cheated him. He left the room and invited someone. Shortly after, Radmilo Bogdanovic came to the office. He was about to resign his ministerial position and Mr. Jovica Stanisic of the DB. That was the meeting when I saw Stanisic again in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened when they arrived to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milosevic asked them what happened to the weapons. And Radmilo Bogdanovic said they had sent 500 pieces to Banija. I said I had no knowledge of that. Radmilo Bogdanovic said, "Well, you're not supposed to know everything." After that, I turned to Milosevic and I told him that there were problems in the functioning of the SUP, that there are insufficient numbers of qualified people, and it was short of people capable of organising internal affairs in Krajina as the competent Secretariat and that we needed criminal scientists, attorneys, those versed in internal affairs so that we could establish the ministry -- that is the secretary of the Interior in a proper way, and he promised to help, and that was the end of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We'll come back to that point that you've just made later in your testimony. But I want to ask you some more questions about the weapons that you learned about at that meeting. After that meeting, at any point, did you learn anything else about those weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that those weapons did not originate from Hungary at all but rather from a warehouse of the TO, and that it was being transported to Krajina under the auspices of Mihalj Kertes and the Ministry of the Interior of Krajina as well as some people in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You say that they came from a warehouse of the TO. Which TO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how did you learn this information?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was in May or June 1991, the then police commander in Knin, who was Martic's aide, and another person from the police station in Knin, I can't remember his name, in any case they take me to the village of Raducic. The other person's name was Milenko Zelenbaba that was the commander of the police station. And Jovo -- I can't remember the last name. They took me to Raducic, close to Knin, and they showed me some weapons in a warehouse. There were rifles, mortars there. They told me those pieces came from Serbia and basically that Braco was kicking his way in to the TO warehouses. When he said "Braco" he had Mihalj Kertes in mind. Later on I heard from Mile Grbic from Bosanski Novi that the weapons that they were carrying over from Serbia was being brought in across Una to Banija and I suppose the sources of the weapons were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a few questions about what you've told us. First of all, Milenko Zelenbaba, he was the commander of which police station?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was he a subordinate of Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And a friend of his as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You mentioned the name Mihajl Kertes. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mihalj Kertes, that's his name. He was up until 1990 and in the course of that year, until the presidential elections in Serbia a member of the Presidency of the Republic of Serbia, and in 1991, I can't remember what his actual role was but he was a close friends and associate of Jovic and Milosevic and his office was at the Presidency building in Serbia, above Milosevic's office.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Instead of Jovic, it's Stanisic, Jovica Stanisic, and not Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Then you mentioned that you learned something from Mil Grbic. Can you tell us again what it is that you learned from him? Mile Grbic, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I used to know Mile Grbic from before, from 1990. He's a man who back in 1990 used to get the weapons from the museum of the memorial park Samarica to Martic in Knin when the barricades were put up in 1990. And that's when he came to see me and that's when I met him. And later on, I met him in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. How do you know that from 1990, that he was doing that in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me himself. He came to Knin and on the occasion of that visit when he was going back, he came to see me. A man brought him along, and he said, "Okay, there are two people here who wish to meet you. Mile Grbic and Zika Rakic were their names and that's how we met. And they said to me that they were in Knin and that the weapons from the museum at the memorial centre Samarica were given to them by the manager of that memorial centre and that they had given all that to Martic and since they were in Knin they took the opportunity to meet me as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where is that memorial centre in Samarica? Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is at the meeting point between Dvor Na Uni, Petrinja, and Kostajnica, the three municipalities, across the river Una, as you go from Bosanski Novi where Grbic used to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know anything about what kinds of weapons these were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just know that the weapons had come from the museum at Samarica. It was the Second World War weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I see. And then moving forward into 1991, did you learn something else from Mile Grbic in 1991 with respect to weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, that's how we became friends. He had a friendly attitude to me because he was the first person who gave me the information which supposedly he received from the Zagreb army zone, that the army was preparing for some events in Croatia and that it would have been a good idea for me to investigate that a little bit. So it was by the end of December or January 1991 he was the first person who told me about that and since he had a cafe in Bosanski Novi, whenever I travelled through, I used to go and see him and take a little break. And in 1991, in August I believe, July perhaps, he told me that weapons were being brought in from Serbia with the assistance of Jovica Stanisic and I asked him what route they took, and he said the motorway. Now, the motorway was going through Croatia, so it was a kind of a riddle from where I stood how they managed to do that or maybe they had another route that he didn't want to reveal to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know where these weapons were going to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Across Una to Banija and Kordun.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what was their end destination? Who was receiving these weapons in Banija and Kordun?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't tell me but at the time the so-called volunteer units, the 7th Banija division and some other volunteer groups were already in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We will talk about those volunteer groups later in your testimony. Yesterday you mentioned the name of Dusan Smiljanic in connection with the arrest of Milan Martic or arrest or detention or -- in September of 1991. Did you know the name Dusan Smiljanic before that event in September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how did you know it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I met him at some point by the end of July, the beginning of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the chief of security of the 10th Zagreb Corps and he came to Korenica together with the corps commander, Nikola Uzelac, at the time when I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you met him, did you learn about anything that he was doing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time, he offered his services in as far as weapons were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what he said, he said in case you need any weapons just get in touch with me, and I'll make sure you get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if he provided any weapons to Serbs in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I sent some people to him, to Zelava [phoen] which is a place not far from Bihac airport, which is partly on the territory of Croatia and partly on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why did you send people to him, for that purpose, of obtaining weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They didn't have any weapons, they stayed everybody else was fully armed and they had nothing and they asked me if I could help them and I remembered him and so I referred them to him in Korenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who were these people that you sent?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were councillors from the municipality of Knin, presidents of local communities in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did they get weapons from Dusan Smiljanic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look please at 65 ter Exhibit 1452?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This appears to be a document from Dusan Smiljanic, a colonel. Is this the same Dusan Smiljanic that we've been speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's addressed to General Ratko Mladic on the 15th of October 1994. I'd like to look at a paragraph. If we could turn to page -- go to page 2 of the B/C/S and it's on page 2 of the English as well at the top. In that paragraph, there, and I think it's easier if I read it for the interpreters, it says, "I illegally established links with leading figures in the SDS in the Lika, Banija Kordun and Banja Luka area and with a group of OB," meaning security organs, or at least identified that way, "and VP," military police, 16, "at the end of April and the beginning of May I began the illegal distribution of arms to Serbian people from what were then our depots and are now the Ustashas'," and various places are identified, "recruiting our Serbian handlers in these depots. This action continued until the beginning of June 1991 by which time about 15.000 assorted infantry weapons, MB, 20 MM PA weapons, and a large quantity of ammunition had been distributed which we judged was decisive in the defence of Lika, Kordun, and Banija, bearing in mind the situation of the operational units which were in the Lika, Kordun and Banija area." Is that consistent with what you've just been telling us about Dusan Smiljanic's role in supplying weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to page 3 of both the English and the B/C/S, about halfway down the page, in the English and about a third of the way down the page in the B/C/S, it's right -- I think that's it. It says, "Given the great opposition and problems in forming the brigade, especially in the Lika area and part of Banija in September 1991, I organised meetings of the most advanced reserve officers and the then representatives of the authorities in Gracac and Vrhovine at which the current president of the RSK, Milan Martic, was present. Following these meetings, a brigade was formed in Gracac, Udpina [phoen], Vrhovine, and Plaski. On the afternoon of the same day I travelled to Novi Grad with Milan Martic intending to resolve some questions about the final capture of Kostajnica. On returning from Novi Grad we were arrested in Otaka village, as you are aware." What do you understand him to be talking about in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's talking about two things basically. First of all, problems having to do with mobilisation of people from the so-called Partizan units, the so-called brigades in September 1991. And secondly, he also talks about the departure for the area of Kostajnica and Novi Grad and his own and Mr. Martic's arrests in Otaka in September 1991 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what the problems were having to do with the mobilisation of people in September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two problems there. First of all -- well, let me first say that those were JNA units, which used to call themselves Partizan brigades, which in military speech or jargon means light brigades. The first problem was that Croats did not respond to mobilisation and did not wish to join those brigades and the problem with Serbs had to do with the fact that talking about Partizans for them smacked of the Partizans in the Second World War and that's why Serbs didn't want to answer the call for mobilisation, and therefore, political action was organised in municipalities amongst the population, and attempts were made to complete this mobilisation. And he mentions that he was working on that together with Mr. Martic in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be received into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 206, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher I'd like to show the witness two more articles. This one I actually have a translation. If the English could be put on the ELMO and the translation given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is an article from the 3rd of April 1991, from Tanjug. You've already told us what Tanjug is. And I'm just going to read the last paragraph and you can read it, Mr. Babic, in the translation that you have in front of you. "Martic expressed his conviction that Slobodan Milosevic will arm the Serbs in Croatia. In view of the fact that the Croatian state has armed the Croats, it is normal for the Serbian state to arm its people to establish a balance. Martic said that 30.000 people from Krajina have volunteered so far to defend Krajina and Knin." Was that consistent with some of the statements that you were reading in the media at that time, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And for the record, this is ERN R0293885. And if this could be given -- be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 207, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And again with the assistance of the usher if I could show one more article. I don't have a translation of this one but if it could just be put on the ELMO. Could it be pushed up just so that it could be read, all -- perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is an article from the Toronto Star on May 11th 1991, it's ERN number 04675487. And I'll just read about halfway down. It says, "leaders of Croatia's rebellious Serbian minority also welcomed the agreement." There is discussion about an agreement at that time. "But police chief Milan Martic said that rebel Serbs would not bow to the Presidency's command to hand in weapons until Croats did so." Mr. Babic, what do you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not getting any translation, I'm afraid. Now I do hear it in my own language but could you please repeat because all I could hear was you reading it out in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Of course I'll repeat it. It says, this is from May 11, 1991, from the Toronto Star, and it's an article in reference to a peace pact or peace agreement at that time and it says "leaders of Croatia's rebellious Serbian minority also welcomed the agreement but police chief Milan Martic said that rebel Serbs would not bow to the Presidency's command to hand in weapons until Croats did so." What do you understand that to be about? You got the translation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. This follows the events, the escalation of events on the 2nd of May and the beginning of May 1991 in general, when there were major incidents and conflicts and bloodshed in the area of Borovo Selo, the surroundings of Knin, Zadar, a large area of Krajina, and the Presidency of Yugoslavia intervened and organised a cease-fire and the start of a political dialogue. This is the period of time that this information refers to. And this is Mr. Martic's stance in relation to those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 208, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you've testified a number of times, you've spoken a number of times in your testimony, about a camp that was set up in Golubic in March or April of 1991. You also testified in -- you also testified about your meeting in March of 1991 with Mr. Milosevic where you asked for assistance for the Ministry of the -- or rather the Secretariat of the Interior, as it was called at that time, in the SAO Krajina and asked for professionals and he said he would give you assistance. After that meeting, what kind of assistance did you get?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't get the kind of assistance that I expected in terms of expert assistance in setting up the Secretariat of the Interior. People came along who basically pursued the militarisation of the police force in Krajina and that was the kind of assistance provided by Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say the militarisation of the police force in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the police force was turned into a paramilitary force or a military organisation following that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter Exhibit 56, which is in evidence as Exhibit 29. Mr. Babic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's the order of the executive council of the SAO Krajina dated the 1st of April 1991, and it was issued by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And again that's the day after the events in Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This document has two parts to it, an order and a conclusion or a request. The order is for mobilisation of the Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina. Why did you order that and did it have any effect?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in response to the events at Plitvice and following our impression that Croatia was -- that the Croatian armed forces were involved in an attempt to occupy Krajina. It was a call for an uprising rather than a real mobilisation because we didn't have the actual preconditions for a true mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did it have any effect? Did it result in anything?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The second part is a request to the government of Serbia that the forces of the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia provide technical and personnel support to the SUP of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina. Why did you make that request?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to honour the terms of our agreement with Milosevic, in order for him to live up to his promise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does this refer to the promise that he made to you in -- when you met with him in March of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you told us a moment ago that the -- what happened after these requests for assistance is in fact the militarisation of the police in the Krajina. Can you explain how that occurred? What happened specifically, concretely?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April, a training camp for Special Forces of -- for special police forces was set up, and it remained in operation throughout the spring and the summer of 1991, and that's where special units used to train, and those were special units from the Krajina Police force, and they would go to various parts of Krajina, various municipalities, when -- and they were deployed there and they increased their numbers. There was a camp in that youth centre and camp at Golubic. Afterwards, near Benkovac, and a similar sort of thing at Samarica, but I don't have any specific information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
