utterances.text: Just for the assistance of the Chamber, the Golubic can be found on page 25 of the atlas. And I believe the witness has already testified that it's a few kilometres from Knin, just north of Knin. Mr. Babic, I want to talk about the Golubic camp. Who set up that camp, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That camp was set up by the secretary of the Secretariat of the Interior of Krajina, Martic, with the assistance of the state security of Serbia, Captain Dragan, and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was there, and they told me as much. In fact, I visited and they reported to me to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How many times did you visit the camp in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Tell us about the first time that you visited. When was it? And who did you see there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first visit was in April 1991, middle of the year maybe, I don't know the exact date. I was actually going to visit Belgrade and somebody from the police station told me to stop by Golubic, and on the way --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have just have to interrupt you because there may have been a slight misunderstanding with the translation. When did that visit occur?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first half of April, maybe mid-April, not later, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry to interrupt. So somebody from the police station told you to stop by Golubic and so what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I stopped by and went there in a small cabin called commander's lodge because it used to be the place where the commander of the labour action was housed, I met the then secretary of the SUP of SAO Krajina, and some men I didn't know who were with him. And then Martic told me the man next to him was Captain Dragan, that he had come to help train the special police forces, and he told me a rather long story about who Captain Dragan was, how he had come to be there, and it was rather bizarre so I didn't really understand. I understood that he had come from somewhere abroad, Martic was mentioning Obrovac, some political parties. It was not a very consistent story but the bottom line was that it was some sort of specialist and that he would be engaged in the training and that that place was going to be the special training centre. I wasn't particularly impressed by the whole thing. They were just sitting around a table in that small lodge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you see any training? Did you see anybody being trained?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing was going on there. They were the only ones who were there, sitting in the commander's lodge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you learn anything more on that occasion in terms of what the purpose of the training was going to be, who was going to be trained there, and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they said that special police units would be trained there. They called them specialists, in shorthand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, what was the second occasion for you to go to Golubic? When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second time was in May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came there and in that little cabin or lodge where the headquarters of the camp was located, I found Franko Simatovic, Nikola Amanovic and some other men. Nikola Amanovic was Martic's assistant at the Secretariat for internal affairs. On the training ground that was just further away from those cabins, there were men involved in drills, policemen, men in camouflage uniforms undergoing training exercises. And they explained to me what the training consisted of and who was being trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did they tell you about that, about what the training consisted of and who was being trained?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Nikola Amanovic told me that groups were all municipalities were coming in, a certain number of people from each municipality, either from the police force or from outside the police force, and underwent training from some -- for some time. They acquired military skills, obtained weapons, and underwent ideological training in some way, and after that they returned to their localities in Krajina. They also showed me a file system containing lists of people for each municipalities and the dossiers on each person undergoing train there, since I was president of the Knin municipality, I asked, "By the way, is there anybody from Knin here?" He said, "Yes, we do have some men." He opened the Knin file and showed me a list of names. The names were not familiar. I don't remember them. That's what I learned at that office on the training ground there was Captain Dragan or one of his assistants maybe, I couldn't see very well, and there were men on the training ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you for a moment. I want to ask you a few questions of the first of all, is the name Nikola Manovic or Nikola Omanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's actually Amanovic, A-manovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. And you mentioned that part of the training was ideological training. Do you know what that consisted of? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people were taught not to be too strongly attached to political parties because they would be working for the state involved in defence. Their primary loyalty should be to the state. It was some sort of military police drill. I don't know what else to call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you understand what Captain Dragan's role was going to be at the camp?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an instructor, a specialist for training, drills, exercises and formation of units. He even formed a standing unit that he was in command of himself. It's the unit called Knindzas. We have already referred to it, and at that time he was its commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. You told us about the Knindzas yesterday in your testimony. What did you understand Frenki Simatovic's role to be at the camp?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he acted as some sort of host there, maybe supervisor, a senior person there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did you understand to be Milan Martic's role at the camp, if any?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was the secretary in the Secretariat of internal affairs. That was his job. He led the administration of the camp or rather his assistant was in charge of the administration of the camp and he was overseeing the whole camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to people once -- after they were trained at the camp? Where did they go? What became of them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would go back to municipalities to form special police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was kept informed and I saw one inspection of a unit that took place near Vrhovine. Martic inspected the unit. It was in July, maybe, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you were telling us about the second visit to Golubic. What happened when you left the camp? Did you go somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frenki took me to show me the target range on the camp-ground, a depression between Udalic [phoen] -- it was actually a target range where trainees at the camp had target practice and he showed me the targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just going to interrupt me for a moment. You have to slow down a little bit because the interpreter is having a little trouble keeping up with you. Where was this target range located?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the right-hand side of the road between Golubic and Strmica village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Chamber, that Golubic Strmica road is evident in the atlas on page 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So did you go to the target range with Frenki Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And towards the end of that valley there were targets standing and somewhere in the middle of that meadow, there was a multi-barrel anti-aircraft gun. There were no men on the range at that moment. Frenki just showed me that anti-aircraft gun. It was either with two or three barrels. And he told me that his men used that gun to shoot at Croatian policemen on the 2nd May in Borovo Selo. It was later built on to the armoured train that Frenki manufactured in Strmica. It was mounted on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that armoured train?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a short train consisting of a diesel locomotive and several cars, two or three maybe. It was reinforced with metal plates and some other types of reinforcement, sandbags. It was provided with an anti-aircraft gun, and it was used as a combat weapon. On the railway between Drnis and Knin and towards Zadar. It was a combat, armoured train. It was not built to perfection. It was not very sophisticated, not the kind you see in movies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How do you know that Frenki manufactured that train?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he showed me that they were doing it, and he asked me to write a letter to the factory producing screws in Knin, to enable him to get metal plates and some other material for building their train. That's the same factory that Milosevic had earlier saved from bankruptcy, that he was financing, and they were kind of indebted to him and had to return the favour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know who paid for the camp at Golubic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that much himself in August 1991, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think you've spoken about this but could you remind us again about that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I talked to Stanisic in Belgrade after Captain Dragan and Frenki were withdrawn from Knin. He invited me to have coffee with him at a restaurant. Maybe he wanted to patch things up a bit, to justify himself. I don't know. He even took his wife along because she was originally from Knin and I suppose he wanted to create a more intimate atmosphere, a friendlier atmosphere. So we met in that restaurant called Seher in Belgrade and on that occasion he was full of criticism for Captain Dragan. He didn't even mention Frenki. So I thought that they wanted to make Captain Dragan a scapegoat for all the resistance they offered to me earlier. And he told me that they had given a large amount of money to Captain Dragan for the funding of the Golubic camp. However, after he had been withdrawn, he had taken the money with him, and from that time on, they were chasing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long did the camp exist at Golubic? You said it was established in April 1991. How long was it in existence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, until August 1991. I don't know exactly when. But in August 1991, there was no training, only depots or maybe there was still some training but to a lesser extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You also spoke about some other camps. Where were they located, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them was in Brgud village on the outskirts of Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know of any others?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of another training centre on Samarica hill but I don't know its exact structure or how it operated. Later on, it became the command post for various agencies or units, or maybe it was already a command post at that time. Samarica is in Banija.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The training camp in Benkovac, did you -- do you know anything more about that? Did you go there or did you just hear about it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I passed by on one occasion, and I stopped in Benkovac. It could have been July 1991. Captain Dragan was in charge of training there. It was a similar camp to Golubic near Knin. There were some installations and training grounds. In the woods, overlooking the village. I don't know exactly where but it's on the outskirts of Benkovac. Maybe the name of the village is Bukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, yesterday you testified, either yesterday or the day before, you testified that you promoted Milan Martic to be the Minister of Defence in May of 1991 because he was neglecting some of the basic tasks and duties of the secretary, that is to protect public order. I want to show you another article and ask you to comment on it, please. Again, I'll need the assistance of the usher, if it could be placed on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, is this document that's on the screen, executive board of the Serb Autonomous Region of April 1991, is it already in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. It's Exhibit number 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If the usher could just push it up a little more, a little bit more, right there, per affect. Leave the date on, please. Just pull it down now, just a bit so that we can see the date. There, that's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is an article from the BBC and the source is the Yugoslav news agency. The date on the top is April 10th, 1991 though the report appears to be from April 8 of 1991. The article concerns bomb attacks on a restaurant in the village of Relo Koleniko [phoen] owned by a Croatian couple. And it talks about a statement made by Milan Martic to the Tanjug journalist, and in the second paragraph it says that Mr. Martic is quoted as saying, "The Knin police force is so busy with the Defence of the Krajina borders and the protection of the Serbian people from the Croatian Ministry of -- for internal affairs that it simply cannot spend more time solving this type of criminal activity. But it is working on it and more will be revealed soon." Is this consistent with what you told us in your -- earlier in your testimony about your view that Mr. Martic was neglecting some of his duties as secretary of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's precisely what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 209, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, yesterday you stated that starting in the spring of 1991, when Martic was promoted in the press and started making more statements in the press, that one of the things he talked about was prisoners who were taken and I believe you said Croatian police who were taken prisoner. Do you know where these prisoners were held?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. Those policemen were held first at the police station in Knin and later in the building of the old hospital in Knin as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher I'm going to show you two more articles. And for the record this is ERN 04675490 to 5491. This is an article from the Toronto Star, June 26, 1991. If we could put the second page on, please, of the article? I'll read the second and third paragraph on that page. "Militant Serbs in Knin, capital of the Krajina region, are holding another 120 Croatian police officers in jail as hostages. They want the government in Zagreb to free Serbs held in March after rioting in a national park. Milan Martic, Serbian chief of police in Knin, said more Croatians would be abducted, 'We are enlarging the prison for future inhabitants,' he said." Do you recall statements like that being made which Mr. Martic in the media at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 210, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have one more article with the assistance of the usher. This is ERN for the record 04675492. This is an article dated July 5th, 1991. It's a report in the BBC but it -- the headline is Belgrade Radio reports Martic's claim of 30 killed in Ljubovo. I'm just going to read the last two sentences of the article. "According to Milan Martic eight Croatian policemen were captured in Dvor Na Uni and sent to the Knin prison from Dvor Na Uni. The prison now contains 42 members of the MUP of Croatia." Is that consistent with the reporting that you were hearing at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew about captured policemen. I don't remember the exact number. But yes, I knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 211, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to move into a new topic which is the attack on Kijevo on the 26th of August 1991, and so perhaps it's a convenient time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for the extra minutes that you gave us. We will adjourn and come back at half past 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you start, Mr. Whiting, the Chamber just wants to indicate that it received the Defence's response to the Prosecution's motion on cross-examination yesterday. We are aware that we are moving fast towards cross-examining the witness, and yet we are unfortunately not in a position just to give the decision just now or today. We will do it first thing on Monday. Will that be okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I actually anticipate that we will file a brief - very brief, maybe one page - reply to the Defence response with leave of the court and that will be done today. It will be no more than a page, Your Honour, and -- but the Monday is fine for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So I can withdraw the apology from the Bench because you're still going to come up with a response?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, as I indicated before the break, I want to ask you some questions about Kijevo. You've told us earlier in your testimony that there it was an attack on Kijevo on the 26th of August 1991 and that this marked a change in the strategy of the JNA. Before we talk about that I want to go back in time a little bit to talk about events that occurred in Kijevo earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I'd like to look, please, at 65 ter 244 and specifically 020 -- I'm sorry, 02170644. Could we scroll down a little bit more just so that's -- perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It appears to be a document from the 3rd of March 1991, from Milan Martic to the Presidency of the SFRY and to the federal SUP and the MUP of Zagreb. Talking about some events in Kijevo at that time. And specifically, it refers to a blockade or a barricade that was set up by armed inhabitants, civilians, from the same village, an event that occurred at the blockade. Do you know anything about what's being talked about in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know of those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before I ask you about them, I would just -- for the benefit of the Chamber, the -- this village, Kijevo, is visible on page 25 of the atlas. It's to the south of Knin. What was going on at this time? What is being talked about in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a response by the Kijevo residents to the events prior to that day in the environs of Kijevo. Since August 1991, August 1990, Kijevo being a Croatian village in the municipality of Knin, there were barricades set up between Kijevo and other areas. And it was difficult for the local residents of Kijevo to travel elsewhere. At a certain point, they did the same. That is, they blocked the roads, and these events are a direct result of the events prior to that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm advised that the document has already been admitted as Exhibit number 105. The question is do you want the English version or --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There is a little -- this is -- there is -- a little bit of confusion create because there are three documents that are in this number and they've -- it appears that they've all been admitted under -- as Exhibit 105. I thought only one of the three but that's fine. If it's in evidence, it's in evidence. I don't need to press that further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The next document is also from 65 ter Exhibit 244, and it's ERN 02170645 and this may also be part of Exhibit 105. And I'm sure I'll get a nod if that is -- yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic --.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We are going to have to scroll down because he can only see the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is a press release from Milan Martic on the 25th of April 1991. It's already in evidence. I'm just going to read the beginning of it. "After the battalion of hats of MUP RH, ordered by the leadership, tried armed aggression on Plitvice and was defeated, the MUP of Republic of Croatia has insisted on making excess situations by directing incidents in the villages inhabited by Croatian people on the region of SAO Krajina. It has been done to convince Yugoslavian and international subjects that the police and repressive action is needed and justified in order to pacify Serb people on Serb ethnical territory of Krajina". Were -- Mr. Babic, if you know, were the Croatian authorities provoking conflict at that time, in that area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. After the events mentioned in the previous document, Croatia established a police station in the village of Kijevo. There was no battalion defeated at Plitvice. This is perhaps pictured as an image that is not completely realistic but I believe that the underlying issue was actually the problem posed by the formation of the police station in Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you told us that Kijevo was a Croat village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, let's move ahead in time now to August of 1991. Before the attack on Kijevo, was there an ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was. That was Mr. Martic's ultimatum issued at the administration of the police, and the inhabitants of the local commune, that they should leave, otherwise they would get hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter Exhibit 115, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say this was already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour, it's already part of Exhibit 105.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a document, rather a statement I heard for the first time given via the media in Knin on the 18th of August 1991. This is Mr. Martic's ultimatum issued to the police administration of Split and the local commune of Kijevo as well as the police station in Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now if we could just scroll down a little bit on the document, there, there, I think that will show it, I'm going to read just from the middle of the page of the English and it's the middle of the page also of the B/C/S. The ultimatum reads, "You have a police station in the village of Kijevo in Knin municipality. This ultimatum is to warn you that our forces will attack this police station at a time we find appropriate if your police forces do not withdraw from this village within 48 hours from the moment of receipt of this ultimatum." And it goes on, "We also want to advise the population of Kijevo to find safe shelters on time so there should be no casualties among them." How did you understand this ultimatum at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took it quite seriously as a warning to the residents of Kijevo to leave, together with the police, and those are actually the opening remarks of the communique mentioning the increased tension between the Serbs and Croats. At the beginning of the communique, Mr. Martic states that the relations between Serbs and Croats have reached such a level that the two people can no longer live together in the territory. Therefore, this was an ultimatum issued not only to the police station but to the residents of Kijevo as well. That's how I understood that and that's why I publicly reacted concerning the communique.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did you publicly react? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Via the media, I stated that the armed forces of Krajina will not break the truce that was in place at the time, and that was accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 212, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarification to me, can I ask one or two questions on this document? You said, Mr. Babic, that the village of Kijevo was a Croat village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were there any Serbs living in Kijevo, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think there was a single Serb house or maybe one at the most. In short, my answer would be no. There were no Serbs in Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, how did you first hear about an attack on Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it for the first time because I was told by a driver or somebody who was in my entourage in Belgrade on that day, in the afternoon, when the attack was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before you learned about the attack, did you have a meeting with Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the same day, after the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Milosevic asked me to come to Belgrade, to come and see him. So I did. And during the meeting, he said that Frenki should go back to Krajina, that he was a good man and he praised him. I already explained that the other day. And that's when I learned from him that Franko Simatovic was the head of the second department of the State Security Service. If need be, I can go through the entire meeting again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. Was there any conversation that related to this -- to the attack on Kijevo in any way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that part of the conversation, I asked questions about the protection of the Serb village Otisic between Vrlika and Sinj. It was a Serb village and there were certain incidents, provocations, as the story was among the Serb, and those incidents were created by the Croatian police searching Serb houses and looking for weapons amongst the Serb population of the village. That was an issue that irked the Serbs there. I expressed those concerns to Milosevic and I asked him to do something to protect the population. I supposed it could have been done the way it had been done before that, that is to deploy the JNA in the buffer zone surrounding Otisic, between Vrlika and Otisic on one side and on the other between Vrlika -- Sinj and Otisic. After my explanation, Milosevic said, "Has that not been dealt with by now?" And I said, "I don't know." And that was the end of it. When I left, I was told by someone there that early that morning, the army attacked Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After you learned that the army had attacked Kijevo, did that give you any understanding about what the remark from Mr. Milosevic might have meant?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day, I was back in Knin, and I went through the area because that's where my house is, where my parents and grandparents lived, as well as the parents of my wife, and I went there to see what was happening. Therefore, I'd been to the area a day after the attack. I reached Vrlika and I passed through Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think you may have misunderstood my question. After you learned about the attack on Kijevo, by the army, did that affect in any way your understanding of what Mr. Milosevic had said in the meeting with you, when he said, "Hasn't that problem been taken care of? Or dealt with by now?"

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had been dealt with the way that wasn't the ordinary way used until that time. Therefore, my understanding of how the situation was dealt with was different from what it may have been in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you said that your family lived in the area. Can you tell us more specifically where in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mother and grandmother lived in my native village of Kukar on the outskirts of Vrlika and my parents -- my wife's parents lived in Vrlika which is a place between Civljane and Otisic in the territory of the municipality of Sinj. That is the territory controlled by the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, who -- do you know who participated in the attack on Kijevo on the 26th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th Knin corps units as well as the JNA units, the police of Krajina and the local TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just so there is no confusion on the record, I think I can clarify the answer. The 9th Knin Corps, they are JNA units, are they not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So the attack was done by the 9th Knin corps, the police of the Krajina and the local TO, am I understanding your answer correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that you went -- you passed through Kijevo on the following day. What did you see?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that the village was destroyed, and some units of the Knin corps deployed along the road. From the point when one enters Kijevo up to Vrlika next to the road there were units of the police battalion of the Knin corps of the JNA, and in Civljane, there was a column of armoured vehicles of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that the village was destroyed. Can you be more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could see damaged houses, houses damaged by shells, either from guns or tanks, that is artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did the damage to the houses compare to the damage to the police station in Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seemed to me that the surrounding houses sustained more damage than the station itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if anything happened to the houses in Kijevo in the days following the attack?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were being plundered and torched.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who was doing that, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The residents of the neighbouring villages and some uniformed people. The village was unprotected, and the plundering was done by whoever was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was this -- when you refer to the residents of neighbouring villages and uniformed people, can you identify the ethnicity of these people who were engaging in the plundering?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did something happen to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt? When you say "uniformed people," what do you mean, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Reservists from JNA units or the TO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What about police? Do you know if police engaged in that activity as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What activity?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that uniformed people engaged in plundering and His Honour Judge Moloto asked you which uniformed people and you said reservists from the JNA units or the TO, and my question is what about the police? Do you know if the police engaged in plundering as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did something happen to your house and your family during this event?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the Croatian police and armed forces were issued an order to kill the members of my family, and they also torched my native house in the village. My mother and grandmother fled, and they killed my father-in-law in his house in Vrlika. My mother-in-law managed to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, how do you know that there was an issue ordered?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that by a JNA officer who was in Civljane, in the JNA unit there. He said that they intercepted a radio communication between the armed forces, between the Croatian national corps guard and the police, and that they overheard that an order was issued for them to kill members of my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why, if you know, would such an order be issued, with respect to your family?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose out of vengeance with regard to myself. I was a Serb politician in Krajina and everybody knew me, and my family lived on the Croatian territory, on the territory under the control of the Croatian government. Probably they took the opportunity when the war started to take revenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know why the JNA and TO and police forces attacked Kijevo? What was the reason for attacking Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the so-called deblocking action for barracks and military facilities in Croatia had already started, and it was the Croatian forces that were involved in that, following orders from the Croatian government, and it was a process that regarded all of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I follow something here? Are you saying, Mr. Babic, that there is no connection between this attack and this warning that was sent to the Split police administration, Kijevo police station, and Kijevo local commune? Is that attack not a follow-up on this warning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would like to say, in reply to your question, that this ultimatum and this provocation that followed from the local TO militia afterwards was an agreed trigger for the JNA to start their own offensive. So it had been a concerted effort which started with this ultimatum and then went on to develop into this offensive by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: There is something that I would like to clear up as well at this stage. Mr. Babic, you had said earlier that there was not a single Serb family in Kijevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: But your family lived in Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Oh, I stand corrected, then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They lived at a distance of about 10 kilometres in another village. There were two villages in between, in fact, so it is further away from Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you've explained that the -- that the relationship between the ultimatum and the attack on Kijevo, but in response to my question about why was there an interest in attacking Kijevo, what was the goal, you responded -- you gave us a response which I've now lost on my screen but I'll get back, concerning deblocking and I'm not quite clear on what your response was, what you were trying to explain there. You talked about deblocking action for barracks. What does that have to do with Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the attack on Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So this is something that followed the attack on Kijevo, the deblocking action?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The explanation as to why the JNA started the offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And can you explain a little bit further what this deblocking was about? What was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian government at some point during the summer 1991 ordered the blockade of the military facilities in Croatia in order to immobilise the JNA and defuse their power and prevent them from intervening and interfering in the political conflict that was in the making on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, especially since Croatia had declared independence and they were waiting for the expiry of this three month moratorium, as it were, for that decision to come into effect and these three months represented a preventive measure, and they department want their decision to be interfered with by the JNA. And therefore the government of Croatia started a blockade, a siege, of the army facilities throughout Croatia. This was done by the citizens of Croatia and the ZNG forces and police. The ZNG forces are the Home-Guard Corps. And they basically organised a siege of the JNA barracks and warehouses and any other military facilities throughout Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And after the attack on Kijevo, did the JNA start an effort to deblock some of these barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And after that, a more broad-based action of JNA was organised in different places, Sinj, Sibenik, Zadar, and also regarding some military warehouses near the Petrinja garrison in Banija, as far as I've heard. So that was what was happening in the area in and around Krajina, the things I know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me return to Kijevo. Do you know if Milan Martic was involved in the attack on Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I heard that he participated, and I saw a clip on television. I saw him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you see on the clip on television?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that when Kijevo was taken, together with the police chief from Knin, Milenko Zelenbaba, he removed the Croatian flag from the police station at Kijevo and he trampled on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you see -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm only doing it because I still haven't mastered the art of bringing back information that has gone out of the screen. I would like to understand what Mr. Babic means by "broad-based action of the JNA." He says -- he said to an answer, "and after that attack on Kijevo did the JNA start an effort to deblock some of these barracks?" Answer: "Yes. And after that, a more broad-based action of JNA was organised in different places, Sinj, Sibenik, Zadar and also regarding some military warehouses." I don't understand what is meant by this broad-based action.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, if you heard the question from His Honour, could you explain what is meant by -- what did you mean by a more broad-based action?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, what I meant by saying broad-based was in terms of the area, the space, and the lifting of the siege was done through the deployment of the JNA units along different axes and with as much military power as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the action is the lifting of the siege, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Lifting of the siege.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Going back to Kijevo, I just told us about seeing a clip on television with Milan Martic and Milenko Zelenbaba. Did you see any other media reporting of the attack on Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a report -- I remember an interview with a reserve officer of the JNA who talked to a Croat inhabitant of Kijevo who remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what do you remember about that interview?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the soldier asked this old man, "Did you kill my grandfather in 1941?" And the old man tried to defend himself and he said, "No, no, I didn't." And, well, that was the gist of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did that have any effect on you? Did you have any reaction to seeing that interaction?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was extremely sad. I myself was horrified. This is the most horrific way of bringing the past and the present together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You referred to a Croat inhabitant who remained there. What did you observe when you went to Kijevo the day after the attack, about -- what did you observe in terms of Croats? What happened to the Croat population in Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village was deserted. There was nobody in the vicinity. And I heard from the people who were there, the soldiers, I mean, what happened, and they said everybody fled in two directions, either across Kozjak or Dinara. So they took to the mountains and then across these mountains they crossed over to the territory under the Croatian control.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did they ever return to Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for as long as the SAO Krajina existed. They didn't until August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you referred to some Croat residents who -- inhabitants who remained. What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some left over the coming years. There were also some murders, some people were killed in precisely that village, some unclarified and unsolved murders. It was never discovered who actually killed those people. Very few people remained, just a couple of old men, that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, the day that you went through Kijevo, the day after that you've already spoken about, did you see any commanders?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, I saw the commander of the brigade of the 9th Corps, Lieutenant or Lieutenant Colonel Djukic, who was the commander of mixed armoured mechanised unit, and he gave me two vehicles in order for me to be able to collect my father-in-law's body, since he had been killed, and he told me that Lieutenant -- that Colonel Mladic had gone on ahead with a unit through Vrlika from the other side of Otasic in the direction of Sinj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you return to Kijevo or the area in the days that followed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because on the first day, I simply went as far as my late father-in-law's house and on the next day I went to see my own family home and my mother and grandmother, and that was in a village behind Vrlika, and I came across Ratko Mladic as I was on my way, and he was leading a group of observers, and I think that there was a representative of Croatian parliament there and a Croatian delegation from Sinj, and he was going to show Vrlika to them once it had been taken by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was Vrlika a Serb village, a Croat village, or a -- mixed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, after these events in Kijevo, and you've already testified about how this represented a change in the approach of the JNA and you've started to talk about events that occurred afterwards, but I want to ask you about chain of command over armed groups in -- armed Serb groups in Croatia, in the Krajina, and we've heard about a number of different groups, the JNA, the police, the TO. After August of 1991, can you explain what the command structure was over these groups? How did it function?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were two chains of command with regard to these armed groups on the territory of Krajina. One line of command went from the General Staff of the armed forces of the SFRJ, that is to say the General Staff command from Belgrade, through the JNA units, and down to the TO. That was one line of command. And the other line of command was the police, the parallel structure in Krajina, the way I called it. There was the state security service of Serbia, the MUP of Serbia, that is, and then the police forces, the militia, in Krajina, the volunteer units, the DB units. That was the second line of command. And at the top of both was Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Below Slobodan Milosevic, on the police side, who was the next in line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Below him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Below him in Krajina, Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the relationship between the police forces, Serb police forces on the ground in the SAO Krajina and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They cooperated closely in combat activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were the police, to your knowledge, resubordinated to the JNA during fighting after August 1991, through the fall?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what's the basis for that answer? Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of my general knowledge, police and -- was never subordinated to either the JNA or the armed forces in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How about the TO and the JNA? What was the relationship between the TO and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the Main Staff of the TO and the zone or area staffs of the TO and the municipal staffs and units. The Main Staff on the TO was in charge of the areas in Northern Dalmatia and Lika and it was under the command of the 9th Corps. And the zone staff of Kordun and Banija was subordinated to the command of the 2nd Operative Group of the JNA at Samarica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So just to be clear about your answer, the TO -- and I'll ask you more about how it was organised in a moment, but the TO in the SAO Krajina was subordinated to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I just want to show you three more articles, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we done with this one document? The document of the 18th of August 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honour, and I believe I moved it into evidence but if I haven't, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm -- yes. I have, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have a translation of this document. If the English could be put on the ELMO and the translation given to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yesterday, you testified that Milan Martic talked to the press about assistance that was being received from the JNA. This is an article from the 7th of July 1991. It's an article in Tanjug. And I'll just read the fourth paragraph. "As regards the aid to Krajina Police, Martic said that the 'most significant aid came from the government of Serbia in nearly all forms,' and that relations with the Yugoslav People's Army were 'very correct' and that coordination with it 'already existed.' It turned out that 'We and the Yugoslav People's Army have a common enemy,' he stressed." And then later a little further down the page a few paragraphs down, it says, "Milan Martic the Krajina Police commander said in another interview to the Titograd daily Pobjeda that the armed group under his command and the army 'are assisting each other.'". And then a little further down it says, "The hardware, arms, and equipment of the army and the Krajina Police 'become common at a given time' because we know who our common enemy is," said Martic. "Martic pointed at the current Croatian authorities as their common enemy, describing them as an 'Ustasha state' which 'does not wish well either to us or the Yugoslav army.'" Now, just so we are clear because we are using different terminology, is the Yugoslav People's Army the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JNA stands for the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Is -- are the statements made in this article consistent with media that you recall from the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 213, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I could again have the assistance of the usher, if it could be placed on the ELMO. This is an article from July 14th 1991 from the Los Angeles Times, and if we could put the third page, make the third page visible, and about halfway down the page, it says -- is it visible to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not right now. It was a couple of seconds ago. It will come. It's there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In the middle there it says -- it's disappeared again. I think if you press the button on again it will come up again. But it keeps going out. Okay. It's up now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It says in an interview, "Knin's police chief Milan Martic said the Krajina had 7.000 police regulars, a reserve force of 20.000 armed with rifles and artillery and what he called 'perfect relations' with the federal army there. 'We have a common enemy in the fascist Croatian forces,' Martic said. 'There have already been many battles.'" . Is this also consistent with statements that you heard at the time in the media?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could that be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 214, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: One more article to show with the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is an article dated the 19th of August 1991, in Tanjug. We can never really rely on technology. It says in the first paragraph, "We will also bring" -- it's a quote, "'We will also bring Petrinja, Karlovac, Zadar under our control because both we and the army apparently share the same interest. We need one major port,' Minister of Defence of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina Milan Martic has told Borba in an exclusive interview." And then later, in the end of the second paragraph, it says, "Martic says that 'last year's raid by the people on the arms depots belonging to police had not been pre-planned.' He believes that the truce has no chance 'because we are also carrying out re-groupings and receiving new supplies of arms in reply to their moves. We have also artillery, our air force, and an army that is on our side and there is nothing to hide about this fact.' Martic also says that he did not even dream he was going to have such military might at his disposal." Now there is an a reference to the truce. Is that the truce that you testified about earlier that was in place in August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is this -- are these statements consistent with what you were hearing in the media at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 215, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Babic, you've testified a number of times about a pattern that was occurring in 1990 and particularly in 1991 with respect to provocations and attempting to draw the JNA into the conflict. I want to focus now on events after August 1991. After August of 1991, were there attacks by Serb forces on Croat villages in the SAO Krajina or around the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you observe a pattern to how these attacks were carried out?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the forces of the police would usually stage a provocation against Croatian-populated areas or the police force on the other side. The Croatian side would respond, after which JNA units would get involved with artillery and they would move into an offensive and advance towards Croatian-populated areas to reach certain positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what would then happen in those villages? What would be the result of the attacks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the same thing that happened in Kijevo. The residents would flee or would be expelled. The houses would be damaged in combat and later looted and torched.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did any individual -- would any Croat civilians remain, and if so, what would happen to them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Few Croat civilians stayed to live there. There was overwhelming uncertainty. People were killed and their murders were not investigated. Civilians were forced to move out of their homes, to Croatian territory. There were mass expulsions of population in some areas such as Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know, after the attack occurred, what the roles of the different forces involved would be in this pattern?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already tried to describe it. The police forces or the parallel structures, as we called them, would stage provocations. JNA units would move in with artillery and launch an attack, and advance. They would be followed by TO militias, volunteer units who would loot and torch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And torch what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Croatian houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did this occur? Where did you see this pattern occurring?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened in the broad area of Krajina. I would continue to see the consequences for months later. Not long after the incidents in Kijevo, a month or maybe two later, I would see the consequences throughout Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you made a reference in your answer, you spoke about volunteers. Can you tell us how volunteers fit into this picture? How were they organised and what relationship did they have with the other units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There existed two types of volunteers. First there were so-called volunteer groups and units formed from the Serb residents of Krajina, or they would form a parallel structure from the DB, the state security service in Banija and in Kordun, the most famous was the 7th Banija division. In August and September 1991, these units reorganised themselves into Territorial Defence units. Another type of volunteers were individual volunteers or volunteer units coming from Serbia. Individual volunteers would join JNA units, and volunteer units acted independently, although I must say there was only one of these in SAO Krajina, whereas in other territories, such as Eastern Slavonia there also existed such units, as units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The one volunteer unit that acted independently, that existed in the SAO Krajina, what was it called, if you know, and where did it function, if you know? Where did it operate?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the largest and the best known, 7th Banija division. It was called. It was active in Banija. That is Dvor Na Uni, Kostajnica, Petrinja, and Samarica. That is the area where weapons were first brought in by Radmilo Bogdanovic, where arms shipments came through Bosanski Novi. That unit resisted for a long time efforts to join the -- to integrate them with the Territorial Defence, once it was formed for the area of Banija, and the unit refused for a long time to subordinate itself to that staff. And its transformation into the TO of Dvor and Kostajnica finally happened after Mr. Martic took over authority over the Territorial Defence. So that this unit became part of the Territorial Defence by end September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. But you also spoke, as I understood it, about individual volunteers or volunteer units coming from Serbia and you said, and I understood this but correct me if I'm wrong, to be different from the 7th Banija division, you said "Individual volunteers would join JNA units and volunteer units acted independently, although I must say there was only one of these in SAO Krajina whereas in other territories such as Eastern Slavonia there also existed other units, as units." What were you referring to when you spoke about one of these in SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In SAO Krajina, that was a unit that had been established by one political party in Serbia, the Serbian renewal movement, and it was active in the area around Gospic in Lika. That was for a while, in September 1991. Whereas in Eastern Slavonia, there was also one volunteer unit called the Serb volunteer guard, under the command of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. It belonged or rather it had a different structure than the former unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the Serbian renewal movement unit that you said was active in the area around Gospic and Lika, do you know if that unit was involved in any fighting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took part in fighting around Gospic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think September 1991, or perhaps October. I can't tell you exactly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Aside from the -- that unit, the Serbian renewal movement unit, were all of the other volunteers that you described subordinated in some way to the JNA by September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Other volunteers, other individual volunteers, were within JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a few minutes early but I'm about to move into another big topic so if it's a convenient time -- or else I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you going to a new topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I am going into a new topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you think it would be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think it would be a convenient time. I think we are back together on Monday morning in Courtroom I, so in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's according to my schedule. Is that how you understand it, Mr. Milovancevic? Courtroom I, Monday morning at 9.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court will adjourn and reconvene on Monday morning at 9.00 in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 20th day of February, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.
